title: Chest pain unit: rapid review of a one-hour troponin rule-out pathway, with a grade withdrawn on re-appraisal
notes: Ordinary path with one explicit null on a model-owned field. The need names a rapid review; a fixture search with few hits returns five records (years 2019 to 2025). The first appraisal grades a conference abstract 'moderate'. The investigator asks for a re-appraisal and the second appraisal call sends the same annotations and claims except that the conference abstract's grade is null (and its limitations explain why): the explicit null must clear that record's grade to 'unrated' with one 'cleared' issue, leave every other grade, the four claims and the overall certainty 'moderate' unchanged, and must not be read as omission (D2, work-order test clear_explicit_null_grade; at 875fe59 the null is logged 'cleared' but the old grade stays, a false cleared log). The null is on a model-owned grade, never on investigator text (G11); the problem reply omits constraints (omitKeys), so the typed constraints stay as entered. The decision (kind narrow) rests on claims c1, c3 and c4 from fully reported records and both gates are met, so acceptance gives accepted and ready. Record ids are stableRecordId(record) from src/lib/evidence/records.ts, computed by the generator: DOI-based for records 1, 3, 4 (ev-0vzr5m5, ev-1iswvrr, ev-0fba4if); title and year for records 2 and 5 (ev-1yix4sd, ev-0joc6ty). Requires D2 (null clears the grade), S13 (appraisal dispatch), S11 (routing basis, selectionStatus, actionStatus) and D5 (decision status text). inputs.need:
I am the clinical lead for the chest pain unit at a 550-bed district general hospital. We see about 9,000 patients a year with suspected acute coronary syndrome, and at present we rule out myocardial infarction with high-sensitivity troponin I at presentation and again at three hours. Patients who are ruled out spend a median of seven hours in the department, and the unit is full most afternoons. The cardiology and emergency medicine consultants want to move to a one-hour rule-out pathway (samples at presentation and at one hour, with early discharge if both are below the assay's thresholds), and the hospital quality committee has asked for a rapid review of the evidence before it approves the change at its meeting on 2 December 2026.

The questions the committee cares about are: how many ruled-out patients have a heart attack or die within 30 days, how many patients can be ruled out at one hour, how much time it saves, and what goes wrong in practice, for example second samples drawn at the wrong time or laboratory delays. I am particularly worried about older patients and people with kidney disease, who make up a large share of our attendances and in whom troponin is often raised for other reasons.

We have six weeks and the clinical librarian can give us about ten hours. There is no funding and we cannot add laboratory staff. I would like a short, honest summary that the committee can act on, not a literature list.

records.title: One-hour high-sensitivity troponin rule-out pathways in the emergency department: a systematic review and meta-analysis of safety
records.authors: Achebe-Lindgren O, Marchetti-Soyinka P, Hallam-Oduya R
records.abstract: We searched four databases to June 2021 for studies applying a 0/1-hour high-sensitivity troponin algorithm to adults presenting with suspected myocardial infarction. Twenty-two studies with 31,400 patients were included. Among patients ruled out at one hour (pooled 57 percent of those tested), the 30-day rate of death or myocardial infarction was 0.3 percent (95 percent CI 0.2 to 0.5). Sensitivity for index myocardial infarction was 98.8 percent. Most studies were prospective validation studies in specialist centres; eight had a high risk of bias in patient selection, and few reported results by age or kidney function.

records.title: Moving from a three-hour to a one-hour troponin pathway in a district hospital chest pain unit: a before-after evaluation
records.abstract: We compared 12 months before and 12 months after a switch from a 0/3-hour to a 0/1-hour high-sensitivity troponin pathway in a 480-bed district hospital. Median time in the department for ruled-out patients fell from 7.2 to 4.1 hours, and the proportion discharged directly from the unit rose from 41 to 55 percent. Among patients discharged after rule-out, the 30-day rate of death or myocardial infarction was 0.4 percent before and 0.3 percent after. In the first three months the second sample was drawn outside the 45 to 75 minute window in 22 percent of patients, falling to 9 percent after a phlebotomy prompt was added.

records.title: Timing of the second troponin sample and laboratory turnaround under rapid rule-out algorithms: an observational study
records.authors: Srinivasan-Holt M, Eriksen-Obi A, Tulloch-Mensah J
records.abstract: Across three emergency departments using a 0/1-hour algorithm, we recorded sample collection and result times for 5,812 patients. The second sample was collected outside the 45 to 75 minute window in 18 percent of patients, most often during the afternoon peak. Median laboratory turnaround was 52 minutes and exceeded 90 minutes for 11 percent of samples. When the second sample was late, the algorithm placed more patients in the observe zone, and 3 of 1,040 late-sampled patients who were ruled out had a myocardial infarction within 30 days. The authors recommend timed prompts and escalation when turnaround exceeds one hour.

records.title: Performance of a one-hour troponin rule-out algorithm in patients aged 75 or over and in chronic kidney disease
records.authors: Beaumont-Adeyinka C, Yamada-Rourke L, Pereira-Strand K, Owusu-Fairley E
records.abstract: In a multicentre prospective study of 9,760 patients, we examined the 0/1-hour algorithm in patients aged 75 or over (n=2,310) and in those with an estimated glomerular filtration rate below 60 (n=1,480). Sensitivity for myocardial infarction remained above 97 percent in both groups, but only 29 percent of older patients and 21 percent of patients with kidney disease were ruled out at one hour, compared with 62 percent of younger patients with normal kidney function. More than half of both groups fell into the observe zone and needed a third sample. Age-adjusted thresholds increased rule-out but lowered sensitivity.

records.title: Early discharge after one-hour troponin rule-out and 30-day outcomes in a regional network: conference abstract
records.venue: Regional Cardiac Society annual meeting abstract book
records.abstract: This abstract reports early discharge after a 0/1-hour rule-out across five hospitals in one region. Of 14,200 patients tested, 7,950 were ruled out and discharged within four hours. The 30-day rate of death or myocardial infarction among them was reported as 0.2 percent. Methods for follow-up were not described, it is unclear whether patients who attended hospitals outside the region were captured, and no full report has been published. Results by age and kidney function were not given, and the abstract does not say how many patients left before the second sample was taken.

response.synthesis: Five retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. A meta-analysis of 22 studies found 0.3 percent 30-day death or myocardial infarction among patients ruled out at one hour, and a district hospital halved time in the department after switching pathways. Second samples drawn outside the timing window are common and push patients into the observe zone. Rule-out at one hour is far less frequent in patients aged 75 or over and in kidney disease, so local time savings depend on the case mix. A regional conference abstract reports similar safety.
response.gradeRationale: Consistent safety estimates from many studies with a narrow interval; downgraded one level because most studies come from specialist centres with younger patients than this unit's, and the local time saving rests on one uncontrolled evaluation.

response.reading: Safety of one-hour rule-out is well estimated where it was studied (claim c1), and a comparable district hospital cut time in the department by about three hours (claim c2). The benefit runs through the proportion ruled out, which is much lower in older patients and kidney disease (claim c4), and through reliable sample timing, which fails often at peak times (claim c3). The laboratory's turnaround and the phlebotomy workflow are therefore as important as the thresholds.

response.overview: Rapid review with stated shortcuts: an update search from June 2021 building on the 2022 meta-analysis, focused on 30-day safety, rule-out yield overall and in older and kidney patients, time in the department, and second-sample timing failures.
response.population: Adults with suspected myocardial infarction assessed with a one-hour high-sensitivity troponin pathway in emergency departments or chest pain units; studies from 2015 in English.
response.exposure: One-hour rule-out pathway (samples at presentation and at about one hour, rule-out below assay-specific thresholds). Comparator where reported: three-hour pathway.
response.procedures: The librarian runs a dated search of three databases from June 2021 and checks the 2022 meta-analysis's included studies. One reviewer screens and a second checks a random 20 percent; one reviewer extracts and a second checks all safety and yield values. Risk of bias is judged with a short tool for accuracy and before-after studies. Conference abstracts are listed but not graded or pooled unless a full report exists.

response.designSummary: Rapid review with random-effects meta-analysis of proportions for safety and yield when at least five studies report them.
response.sampleSize: The unit of analysis is the study. The 2022 meta-analysis pooled about 18,000 ruled-out patients, so a pooled 30-day event rate near 0.3 percent is estimated to within about 0.15 percentage points; the update matters for the age and kidney subgroups, where one study of 2,310 older patients gives a yield estimate within about 2 percentage points. Pooling within subgroups needs at least three studies reporting them.
response.primaryAnalysis: Random-effects meta-analysis of the proportion of ruled-out patients with 30-day death or myocardial infarction on the logit scale, with 95 percent confidence and prediction intervals; certainty rated with GRADE.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Meta-analysis of rule-out yield overall and by age 75 or over and kidney function where reported; time in the department and timing failures summarised as medians and ranges.
response.missingData: No author contact; studies without 30-day follow-up for all ruled-out patients are flagged and removed in a sensitivity analysis.
response.multiplicity: One primary safety outcome; subgroup estimates presented descriptively with intervals.
overfittingGuards: No threshold comparisons beyond those reported
response.summary: Proportion meta-analysis for safety and yield; the update adds precision where it matters, in older and kidney patients.

response.risks: No participants; the risk is an overconfident summary that leads to unsafe early discharge, or an overcautious one that keeps the unit crowded.
response.data: No personal data; search strategy, screening log and extraction sheet archived with the report.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: age over 75, kidney disease, sex (atypical presentations in women) and language barriers can affect both rule-out yield and safety. The review reports results by age and kidney function where available, notes studies that excluded these groups, and asks the committee to monitor time saved for older patients.
response.effectiveness: The review is useful if the committee can see safety, the likely local yield and the practical failure points before approving the change.
response.efficiency: Existing librarian and clinician time only.
response.costs: About ten librarian hours and 12 reviewer days within existing roles.

response.summary: Review of published data with an equity focus on age, kidney disease and sex.

response.title: One-hour high-sensitivity troponin rule-out for a district hospital chest pain unit: a rapid review of safety, yield and sampling failures
response.abstract: Objective: to summarise the 30-day safety of one-hour troponin rule-out, the proportion of patients ruled out overall and in older and kidney patients, time saved, and second-sample timing failures. Design: rapid review updating a 2022 meta-analysis with a dated search from June 2021 and stated shortcuts. Results and conclusions will be written after the synthesis.
response.introduction: One-hour rule-out pathways promise shorter stays, but most evidence comes from specialist centres with younger patients. A district hospital where 38 percent of attendances are aged 75 or over needs to know the likely yield and failure points before adopting one.
response.methods: Three databases were searched from June 2021 and the 2022 meta-analysis's studies were included. One reviewer screened with a 20 percent check; safety and yield values were double-checked. Proportions were pooled on the logit scale with random effects; conference abstracts were listed but not graded or pooled.
response.results: No studies have been screened yet. The report will present the search flow, pooled 30-day safety, yield overall and by age and kidney function, time in the department and timing failures.
response.discussion: The discussion will set the likely local yield against the safety estimate, describe the sampling and laboratory conditions under which the pathway worked, and state what the unit should monitor after any change.
response.limitations: Rapid review shortcuts; English only; subgroup data sparse; one ungraded conference abstract.
response.conclusion: To be written after the synthesis; it will not extrapolate safety to groups the studies did not include.
response.reportingChecklist: PRISMA 2020, with the rapid review shortcuts listed
response.summary: PRISMA-structured draft with results left empty until the synthesis.
